title: Emrys and the Confession
premise: True-crime podcaster Lior Eastwick has spent three years documenting the disappearance of Emrys Vale, a lighthouse keeper's son who vanished from the coastal town of Greyharrow forty years ago. When a confession letter arrives postmarked the day after a stranger's funeral, Lior discovers the dead man was Emrys himself, living under another name, and that his confession implicates someone still alive in Greyharrow — possibly Lior's own estranged mother, who fled the town decades ago. Decoding a ledger hidden in the town's memorial plaques, Lior uncovers that Emrys witnessed a death the town buried and spent his life protecting the wrong person out of love. In the end, Lior must choose between exposing the truth that will destroy their last living family or letting the sea keep its secret.
about_author: Tamsin Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former archivist who grew up in a fading seaside town where everyone remembered things differently. They write mysteries about the stories communities tell themselves to survive.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Lior Eastwick receives an unsigned confession letter postmarked the day after a funeral they didn't attend, referencing details only the vanished Emrys Vale could know. POV: Lior. The beat is unease — the letter names Lior by a childhood nickname no one alive should remember.

chapters.title: The Coldest Case
chapters.summary: Lior reviews their podcast archive on Emrys Vale's 1984 disappearance, realizing the letter quotes phrases from episode seven verbatim — but adds one detail never made public. POV: Lior. The emotional beat shifts from professional curiosity to personal violation: someone inside the story is watching them.

chapters.title: Greyharrow
chapters.summary: Lior returns to the fog-bound coastal town for the first time in fifteen years, checking into a boarding house run by Maren Quill, who remembers Lior's mother all too well. POV: Lior. The beat is displacement — home as foreign country, every street a half-memory.

chapters.title: The Funeral Nobody Claimed
chapters.summary: Lior attends the stranger's funeral and learns the deceased, 'Edwin Marsh,' had no family — yet mourners whisper he'd lived in Greyharrow before under another name. POV: alternating Lior and Maren. The beat is grief without ownership; Maren suspects Edwin was Emrys and fears what that means.

chapters.title: Mother's Silence
chapters.summary: Lior confronts their estranged mother, Sable, by phone; she hangs up when Emrys's name is spoken. POV: Lior. The beat is anger curdling into dread — Sable's fear sounds less like guilt than like warning.

chapters.title: Ledger in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: Following clues in the letter, Lior discovers dates carved into Greyharrow's memorial plaques form a ledger of payments — sums logged against initials, including 'S.E.' POV: Lior. The beat is revelation with vertigo: the town itself is the account book.

chapters.title: What Maren Kept
chapters.summary: Maren confesses she received letters from Edwin Marsh for years and burned most of them, keeping one sealed envelope addressed to 'the Eastwick child.' POV: Maren. The beat is complicity — her loyalty to the town warring with her tenderness toward Lior.

chapters.title: The Night of the Storm
chapters.summary: A flashback chapter reconstructs October 1984 through a recovered diary: teenage Emrys saw something at the old cannery during a storm, something involving two figures and a body that was never reported. POV: Emrys (via diary). The beat is terror frozen in amber.

chapters.title: Initials and Debts
chapters.summary: Lior cross-references the ledger initials with town families and finds the payments stopped abruptly in 1985 — except one line, 'S.E.,' continuing annually until this year. POV: Lior. The beat is narrowing dread: Sable Eastwick has been paying, or being paid, for four decades.

chapters.title: The Constable's Grandson
chapters.summary: Deputy Rhys Calloway, grandson of the 1984 constable, warns Lior off the case — then privately admits his grandfather's files contain a page torn out. POV: Rhys. The beat is divided loyalty; Rhys wants the truth but dreads whose name is on the missing page.

chapters.title: Sable Comes Home
chapters.summary: Sable arrives unannounced in Greyharrow, demanding Lior drop the podcast's final episode. Mother and daughter circle each other in Maren's kitchen. POV: alternating Lior and Sable. The beat is a duel of silences — each hiding something to protect the other.

chapters.title: The Sealed Envelope
chapters.summary: Maren finally hands over Edwin's last letter; inside is a photograph of the cannery, a circled window, and the words 'I confessed to the wrong crime on purpose.' POV: Lior. The beat is inversion — Emrys wasn't confessing to murder; he was covering for it.

chapters.title: Cannery Ghosts
chapters.summary: Lior and Rhys search the condemned cannery and find a hidden room containing a child's belongings and a second ledger — one recording not payments but sightings: someone watched over a hidden person for years. POV: Lior. The beat is wonder inside horror: Emrys wasn't hiding a secret, he was hiding someone.

chapters.title: The Person Who Never Existed
chapters.summary: Records reveal a girl declared dead in 1984 — Wren Calloway, the constable's own daughter — whose death certificate bears Sable's maiden name as witness. POV: Rhys. The beat is shattering kinship: the case runs through Rhys's own bloodline.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: Lior traces Wren Calloway to a woman living quietly inland under a new name, alive because Emrys faked her death and Sable helped smuggle her away. POV: Wren. The beat is fragile peace — a life built on a lie that kept her breathing.

chapters.title: Whom the Letter Accuses
chapters.summary: Rereading the confession with Wren's existence in mind, Lior decodes its true meaning: Emrys confessed to shielding Wren from her father, the constable, whose 'accident' at the cannery was no accident. POV: Lior. The beat is moral collapse — every protector was also a perpetrator.

chapters.title: Rhys's Choice
chapters.summary: Rhys learns his grandfather was the killer and that Wren is his aunt; he must decide whether the law he serves can survive his family's truth. POV: Rhys. The beat is grief weaponized — justice and mercy pulling him apart.

chapters.title: Sable's Confession
chapters.summary: Sable finally tells Lior everything: she helped hide Wren because the constable would have killed her, and Emrys took the blame so a frightened sixteen-year-old wouldn't. POV: Sable. The beat is release — forty years of silence breaking open like a hull.

chapters.title: The Last Episode
chapters.summary: With the final episode due to air, Lior sits with the recording that could free Emrys's name and destroy Wren's safety, while anonymous threats arrive promising consequences. POV: Lior. The beat is the weight of the microphone — truth as a loaded instrument.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Someone breaks into Maren's boarding house searching for the ledgers; Rhys catches the intruder — a retired townsman paid for decades to ensure silence. POV: Rhys. The beat is escalation — the conspiracy is smaller and more human than feared, and cornered.

chapters.title: Emrys and the Confession
chapters.summary: At the cliffside memorial, Lior airs a crafted final episode: Emrys's full story told without naming Wren, exposing the constable's crimes and the town's complicity while preserving the innocent. POV: Lior. The climax beat is catharsis — truth told slant, exactly enough.

chapters.title: What the Sea Keeps
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Greyharrow begins reckoning with its history; Wren visits Emrys's grave at last, and Lior, staying on in town, mails a letter of their own — forgiveness, postmarked today. POV: Lior. The resolution beat is belonging earned: identity chosen rather than inherited.
